title: The price of waiting
bodyMd:
Economic discussions of queues often describe waiting time as a hidden price. When a scarce service is free at the point of use, people may pay with hours rather than money. This observation usefully challenges the idea that a zero fee means zero cost. It does not, however, establish that replacing a queue with a monetary charge is always an improvement. The language of price can clarify one comparison while obscuring another. An hour spent waiting is not equally burdensome for someone who can rearrange a day and someone who will lose a shift. Nor does the same fee impose an equal sacrifice on every household. Expressing both burdens in a common vocabulary does not erase those differences. It instead invites a more careful inquiry into whose resources a mechanism demands and whether those demands are relevant to the public purpose for which the service exists.

Consider a fictional public repair clinic. Retired residents can wait during the afternoon, while workers with inflexible shifts cannot. A queue allocates access partly according to available time. A fee would allocate it partly according to available income. Neither resource is distributed evenly, and the person disadvantaged by one arrangement may not be disadvantaged by the other. Calling time a price identifies a burden; it does not tell us how to compare that burden across people.

There are also institutional alternatives between an unrestricted queue and a high fee. Appointments can reduce physical waiting, but an online booking system may favor those able to monitor it constantly. A lottery can distribute chances evenly among applicants, yet it may fail to prioritize urgent repairs. A priority rule can address urgency, but it needs evidence and a procedure for contested cases. Each mechanism changes both the cost of seeking service and the basis on which access is granted.

The useful question is therefore not which mechanism is costless. None is. It is which combination of burdens and priorities best fits the service's purpose, and whether those burdens are visible enough to evaluate. An argument for charging should show why the resulting allocation is preferable, not merely observe that queues consume time. Similarly, a defense of free access should not ignore the people whom waiting already excludes.
